title: Consent and refusal at 16 and 17: FLRA 1969 s8, MCA from 16 and the courts
blurb: Apply the Family Law Reform Act 1969 and the Mental Capacity Act 2005 to 16 and 17-year-olds, and know when a refusal goes to court.
question: Ollie, 17, has capacity and refuses a blood transfusion that the team believes he needs to survive a major haemorrhage. His mother says she will sign the consent form instead. What should the team do?

teach.body: From 16, two statutes take over from Gillick. The Family Law Reform Act 1969 s8(1) makes a 16 or 17-year-old's consent to surgical, medical or dental treatment as effective as an adult's, so parental consent is then not needed. The Mental Capacity Act 2005 applies from 16, so capacity is presumed and, if lacking, decisions are made in the young person's best interests. In plain English: treat a 16-year-old's consent like an adult's, but remember they are still a child for safeguarding and for refusals of life-saving treatment.
teach.cite: Family Law Reform Act 1969 s8; Mental Capacity Act 2005 ss1-4

teach.caption: MCA s2(5): the Act's powers to act for someone lacking capacity are not exercisable for a person under 16 (subject to s18(3)).

head: Covered
Detail
rows: s8(1): as effective as an adult's consent
teach.caption: s8(3) preserves any consent that would have been effective anyway.
MCA s24(1): an advance decision is made by a person after reaching 18 and with capacity.

teach.h: Refusal: the court, not the parent
teach.body: A capacitous 16 or 17-year-old's refusal of treatment that may prevent death or severe permanent harm can be overruled by the High Court under its inherent jurisdiction (Re W [1992]). Whether a parent's consent can override such a refusal is legally uncertain, so the safe course is to seek urgent legal advice and a court decision, rather than proceeding on a parent's signature against the young person's wishes.

teach.h: A 16 or 17-year-old and a treatment decision
Deprivation of liberty at 16-17: Re D
teach.body: In Re D (A Child) [2019] UKSC 42 the Supreme Court held that it is not within the scope of parental responsibility to consent to living arrangements for a 16 or 17-year-old that would otherwise amount to a deprivation of liberty under Article 5. If a young person lacking capacity has restrictive care arrangements that may amount to a deprivation of liberty, the team raises it with the safeguarding or legal team so that authorisation can be sought from a court (DoLS applies only from 18).

Ollie is presumed to have capacity, and the team has found he understands, retains and weighs the information. His mother's signature is not a safe basis for overriding his refusal of life-saving treatment. The team escalates to the consultant and the trust's legal team for an urgent High Court decision, keeps Ollie involved, manages bleeding with every measure he accepts, and documents the capacity assessment and his reasons.

teach.text: Gillick is the under-16 test. At 16 and 17, use the MCA presumption of capacity: do not 'assess Gillick competence' for a 16-year-old. And a 17-year-old cannot make a legally binding advance decision: that starts at 18 (MCA s24).

items: FLRA s8: a 16 or 17-year-old's consent to treatment, diagnosis and ancillary anaesthesia is as effective as an adult's.
MCA applies from 16: presume capacity; if lacking, act in best interests.
A capacitous refusal of life-saving treatment at 16-17 can be overruled by the court; seek legal advice.
Re D [2019] UKSC 42: parents cannot consent to a deprivation of liberty of a 16 or 17-year-old.
Advance decisions and LPAs are for people aged 18 and over.

summary: You can now apply FLRA s8 and the MCA to 16 and 17-year-olds, and act correctly when one lacks capacity or refuses life-saving treatment. You can also explain why parents cannot authorise a 16 or 17-year-old's deprivation of liberty (Re D).

A.q: Sam, 16, attends day surgery alone for a planned arthroscopy. He has capacity and consents after full discussion. His mother rings to say she must sign too. What is correct?
options: Sam's consent is valid and parental consent is not needed
Both signatures are needed until Sam turns 18 years old
Sam's consent is valid once his mother confirms it by telephone
Sam must first be assessed for Gillick competence
A.why: FLRA 1969 s8(1): a 16-year-old's consent to surgical treatment is as effective as an adult's, and parental consent is not necessary.

whyNot.1: There is no dual-signature requirement at 16 or 17.
whyNot.2: His consent does not depend on his mother's confirmation.
whyNot.3: Gillick applies under 16; at 16 the MCA presumption of capacity applies.

A.q: Amara, 17, is confused after a head injury, cannot retain information about her CT scan and has no parent present. How should the decision be made?
options: Under Gillick, by asking whether she is mature enough
Under the Mental Capacity Act, in her best interests
By waiting until a parent can attend to consent
By applying to the court before any scan is done
A.why: The MCA applies from 16. Amara lacks capacity for this decision, so the scan can proceed in her best interests, consulting family when possible.

whyNot.0: Gillick is the test for under-16s.
whyNot.2: Waiting risks harm; the MCA allows a best interests decision now.
whyNot.3: A routine best interests decision does not need the court.

A.q: Which procedure is expressly included in FLRA 1969 s8 for a 16-year-old's consent?
options: Making an advance decision to refuse treatment
Appointing a health and welfare attorney
Agreeing to a deprivation of liberty for a sibling
An anaesthetic given as part of planned treatment
A.why: s8(2) extends the section to procedures ancillary to treatment, 'in particular, the administration of an anaesthetic', and to diagnostic procedures.

whyNot.0: Advance decisions need the person to be 18 (MCA s24).
whyNot.1: LPAs are not part of FLRA s8 and need the donor to be 18.
whyNot.2: s8 concerns the young person's own treatment, not decisions about others.

B.q: Grace, 17, has cystic fibrosis and capacity. She wants to make a legally binding advance decision refusing invasive ventilation. What should the nurse tell her?
options: She can make one now, if it is written and witnessed
She can make one now, if her parents countersign it
She can make one once she is assessed as Gillick competent
Record her wishes; a binding one must wait until 18
B.why: MCA s24(1): an advance decision is made by a person after reaching 18. Grace's wishes still matter and should be recorded in her care plan.

whyNot.0: Formalities do not overcome the age requirement in s24.
whyNot.1: Parental countersignature cannot create a valid advance decision.
whyNot.2: Gillick does not apply at 17 and does not create advance decisions.

B.q: Luca, 16, has a learning disability. His parents say they always make his health decisions. He needs a dental extraction. What is the nurse's first step?
options: Accept his parents' consent as they hold PR
Assess his capacity, presuming he has it
Apply to the court for a best interests order
Assess whether he is Gillick competent
B.why: The MCA applies from 16 and requires capacity to be presumed. Luca must be supported to decide; a learning disability does not by itself mean he lacks capacity.

whyNot.0: Parental consent cannot be the starting point for a 16-year-old under the MCA.
whyNot.2: A court is not the first step for a routine decision.

B.q: Rhys, 16, is heavily intoxicated in the ED with a clean scalp laceration that can safely wait. He cannot currently weigh information about suturing. What is the best approach?
options: Suture now under MCA best interests, as he lacks capacity
Suture now with consent from either parent by telephone
Wait until he regains capacity, as closure can safely wait
Discharge him and advise his GP to review the wound in the morning
B.why: Under the MCA, consider whether the person may regain capacity and whether the decision can wait (s4(3)). Delayed closure is safe here, so Rhys can decide himself later.

whyNot.0: Best interests includes considering whether he will regain capacity soon.
whyNot.1: At 16 the MCA governs; waiting for his own decision is better.
whyNot.3: Discharging an intoxicated 16-year-old with an untreated wound is unsafe.

C.q: Nadia, 17, has capacity and refuses dialysis that the team believes she needs to survive. Her father, who has PR, offers to consent. There is time to act. What is the best course?
options: Seek urgent legal advice so the court can decide
Accept the refusal, as at 17 it binds like an adult's
Start dialysis on the consultant's best interests decision
Ask the ethics committee to authorise treatment
C.why: A capacitous 16 or 17-year-old's refusal of life-saving treatment can be overruled by the court. With time available, the team seeks an urgent court decision.

whyNot.1: At 17 her refusal of life-saving treatment can be overruled by the court.
whyNot.2: Nadia has capacity, so there is no MCA best interests decision for a clinician to make; only the court can overrule her refusal.
whyNot.3: An ethics committee has no legal power to overrule her.

C.q: Ben, 16, lacks capacity and lives in a residential unit. The trust's legal team advises that his care arrangements would amount to a deprivation of liberty unless validly authorised. His parents tell the nurse they consent to them. What does Re D [2019] UKSC 42 establish?
options: Parents can consent to this for any child under 18
Parents can consent once two clinicians agree
Parents cannot consent to this for a 16 or 17-year-old
Parents cannot consent once he is assessed as Gillick competent
C.why: Re D held that consenting to arrangements that would otherwise be a deprivation of liberty for a 16 or 17-year-old is outside parental responsibility; authorisation must come from a court.

whyNot.0: Re D held the opposite for 16 and 17-year-olds.
whyNot.1: Clinical agreement does not bring this within parental responsibility.
whyNot.3: Gillick does not apply at 16, and Ben lacks capacity.

C.q: Kian, 17, is brought in after an overdose and needs urgent treatment within minutes. He is drowsy, cannot weigh information and no parent is present. What should the nurse do?
options: Wait for a parent to give consent by telephone
Treat now under the MCA in his best interests
Wait for an urgent court order before treating
Ask Kian to sign a form while he is still awake
C.why: The MCA applies at 17. Kian lacks capacity and treatment is urgent, so it proceeds in his best interests.

whyNot.0: Waiting for a parent delays urgent treatment the MCA already permits.
whyNot.2: No court order is needed for urgent best interests treatment.
whyNot.3: A signature from someone who cannot weigh information is not valid consent.

reteach.title: Sixteen: adult consent, child protection
reteach.question: What is different about a 16 or 17-year-old?

blocks.body: For saying yes, a 16 or 17-year-old is treated like an adult: FLRA s8 makes their consent effective and the MCA presumes capacity. For saying no to life-saving treatment, they are still a child: the High Court can overrule. They also cannot make advance decisions or LPAs until 18, and parents cannot consent to a deprivation of liberty for them (Re D).

blocks.text: Use the MCA at 16, not Gillick. Lacks capacity = best interests. Capacitous refusal of life-saving care = legal advice and court.

explain.body: Consent at 16 to surgical, medical or dental treatment is as effective as an adult's. It includes diagnostic procedures and ancillary procedures such as anaesthesia. Parental consent is not needed.

test.q: Lucy, 16, consents to an upper GI endoscopy under sedation to investigate weight loss. A student asks whether s8 covers a diagnostic test. What is correct?
options: No, s8 is limited to surgical treatment
No, diagnostic tests need a PR holder's consent
Yes, if a parent is present to witness it
Yes, s8 includes diagnostic procedures
test.why: s8(2) defines treatment to include any procedure undertaken for diagnosis, and ancillary procedures such as sedation or anaesthesia.

whyNot.0: s8 covers surgical, medical and dental treatment, and diagnosis.
whyNot.1: No PR holder consent is needed when s8 applies.

explain.body: Capacity is presumed. If a 16 or 17-year-old lacks capacity for a decision, act in their best interests, consulting parents and others. Consider whether capacity may return.

test.q: Which statement about the MCA and 16 or 17-year-olds is accurate?
options: Capacity is presumed from the 16th birthday
Capacity is presumed once Gillick is confirmed
Capacity is presumed from the 18th birthday
The MCA applies once parents have been consulted
test.why: Most of the MCA applies from 16, including the presumption of capacity.

whyNot.1: Gillick is not a precondition at 16.
whyNot.3: Consultation is part of best interests, not a trigger for the Act.

explain.body: A capacitous 16 or 17-year-old's refusal of treatment that may prevent death or severe permanent harm can be overruled by the High Court. Seek legal advice early.

test.q: Who can overrule a capacitous 17-year-old's refusal of a life-saving operation when there is time to act?
options: The consultant surgeon
The trust's Caldicott Guardian
The High Court
The Court of Appeal
test.why: The High Court's inherent jurisdiction allows it to overrule a minor's refusal of life-saving treatment.

whyNot.0: A clinician cannot overrule a capacitous refusal.
whyNot.1: A Caldicott Guardian oversees the use of confidential information and has no power over treatment decisions.
whyNot.3: Applications are made to the High Court, not the Court of Appeal.

explain.body: Parents cannot consent to arrangements that would otherwise be a deprivation of liberty for a 16 or 17-year-old. Such arrangements need authorisation by a court.

test.q: Why does Re D matter to a nurse caring for a 17-year-old who lacks capacity and whose care arrangements would otherwise amount to a deprivation of liberty?
options: Parental consent makes the arrangement lawful
Parental consent cannot authorise the arrangement
The young person must personally consent to the arrangement
No authorisation is needed under the age of 18
test.why: Re D held that consent to such arrangements for 16 and 17-year-olds is outside parental responsibility, so the team must seek proper authorisation.

whyNot.0: That was the position Re D rejected for 16 and 17-year-olds.
whyNot.2: He lacks capacity, so he cannot consent.
whyNot.3: Authorisation is needed; parents cannot provide it.
